devices.name: simile
devices.definition: An open comparison: one thing is said to be like another, with a signal word such as 'like' or 'as'.

latin: quae teneram prōlem prōdūxit in āera nīdō
examples.english: like a bird who has led her tender young out of a high nest into the air
just so a shepherd's panpipe rises little by little from reeds of unequal length

devices.name: metaphor
devices.definition: A hidden comparison: one thing is called by the name of something it resembles, with no 'like' or 'as'.

examples.english: by an unaccustomed road he swam out to the icy Bears
and lacking his oarage
the oarage of his wings
with me as guide, pluck your road!
and he believed they were gods, who could pluck the upper air

devices.name: alliteration
devices.definition: The same opening sound repeated in nearby words.

examples.english: but the sky is surely open … let Minos own everything, he does not own the air

devices.name: foreshadowing
devices.definition: A hint early in a story of what will happen later.

examples.english: not knowing that he was handling his own danger
he gave his son kisses that would never be given again

devices.name: rhetorical question
devices.definition: A question asked for effect, not for an answer.

examples.english: 'where are you? In what place shall I look for you?'

latin: ' que 'tibī, lascīve puer, cum fortibus armīs?'
examples.english: 'And what have you to do with strong weapons, naughty boy?'

devices.name: paradox
devices.definition: A statement that seems to contradict itself but is true.

examples.english: but the unhappy father, now no longer a father

devices.name: synecdoche
devices.definition: A swap of part and whole: one thing is called by the name of a part of it (or of the whole it belongs to).

examples.english: 'he may block the lands and the waves,' he says
on swift feathers

devices.name: metonymy
devices.definition: A swap by association: one thing is called by the name of something connected with it (not a part of it).

examples.english: after the last hand was laid on the work
the reminders of unspeakable Venus

latin: īnsuētum per iter gelidās ēnāvit ad
examples.english: by an unaccustomed road he swam out to the icy Bears

devices.name: apostrophe
devices.definition: The speaker turns aside to address someone or something that cannot answer.

latin: partem opere in tantō, sineret dolor,
examples.english: you too, Icarus, would have had a large part in so great a work, had grief allowed

latin: ,' dīxit 'ubi es? quā tē regiōne requīram?'
examples.english: 'Icarus,' he said, 'where are you? In what place shall I look for you?'
returned to these lands first, he dedicated to you, Phoebus, the oarage of his wings

latin: id vitium nūllī per saecula longa notātum—
examples.english: that flaw, noticed by no one through long ages -- what does love not sense? -- you lovers saw first, and you made it a road for your voices
but that beauty of yours forbids you to be what you wish, and your looks fight your prayer

devices.name: ecphrasis
devices.definition: A vivid description of a work of art inside a poem or story.

latin: bis cōnātus erat cāsūs effingere in aurō,
examples.english: on the doors, the death of Androgeos … twice he had tried to shape the fall in gold

devices.name: hendiadys
devices.definition: One idea split into two nouns joined by 'and'.

examples.english: hating Crete and his long exile
we pour offerings from bowls and gold

devices.name: hyperbaton
devices.definition: Words that belong together, such as an adjective and its noun, are split far apart.

examples.english: he spoke, and sends his mind off into unknown arts
he passes on (the rules of flying) and fits the unknown wings to his shoulders

devices.name: chiasmus
devices.definition: Crossed word order, A B B A: the second phrase reverses the first.

examples.english: let Minos own everything; he does not own the air
Pyramus and Thisbe, he the most handsome of young men, she preferred over all the girls the East held
and the more it is covered, the more the covered fire burns
often, when they had taken their places, Thisbe on this side, Pyramus on that
where Semiramis is said to have ringed her high city with walls of baked brick
at once the one loves; the other flees the very name of a lover

devices.name: synchysis
devices.definition: Interlocked word order, A B A B: two adjective-noun pairs woven together.

examples.english: and his mouth, shouting his father's name, is taken in by the blue water
(the sun's sad face) kept offering ghastly light to the troubled lands
the wall shared by both houses
and through it their sweet talk used to cross safely, in the smallest whisper
that a way across has been given to our words, to friendly ears

devices.name: aetiology
devices.definition: A story that explains the origin of something that still exists.

examples.english: is taken in by the water, which took its name from him
he buried him, and the land is called by the name of the boy buried there

devices.name: intertext
devices.definition: One text deliberately echoes another.

examples.english: Ovid: and the father's hands trembled / Vergil: twice the father's hands fell

devices.name: onomatopoeia
devices.definition: A word whose sound imitates its meaning.

examples.english: their sweet talk used to cross in the smallest whisper
(the pipe) splits, and through a narrow hissing hole (shoots out) long (jets)

devices.name: personification
devices.definition: Giving a thing human feelings or actions.

examples.english: 'jealous wall,' they said, 'why do you stand in the lovers' way?'

devices.name: litotes
devices.definition: Understatement by denying the opposite.

examples.english: and we are not ungrateful: we admit that we owe it to you
not otherwise than when a pipe, where the lead is flawed …

devices.name: antithesis
devices.definition: Opposite ideas set against each other in matching form.

examples.english: and the daylight, which seemed slow to leave, plunges into the waters, and from those same waters night comes out

latin: at tū quae rāmīs arbor miserābile corpus
examples.english: but you, tree, who with your branches now cover the pitiable body of one, and soon will cover two
'he may block the lands and the waves,' he says, 'but the sky, surely, is open'
so that, if you fly lower, the water does not weigh down your feathers; if higher, the fire does not scorch them
this one puts love to flight, that one makes it

devices.name: transferred epithet
devices.definition: A describing word that agrees with one noun but describes another.

examples.english: she saw (the lioness) and fled on frightened foot into a dark cave
guiding blind footsteps with a thread
when the boy began to delight in daring flight

devices.name: anaphora
devices.definition: The same word repeated at the start of phrases or lines, one after another.

examples.english: and when he had given tears to the cloak he knew, he gave it kisses
(let them be buried together) whom sure love, whom their last hour joined
but her prayers touched the gods, touched her parents
'Icarus,' he said, 'Icarus,' he said ... 'Icarus,' he kept saying

latin: labor ille domūs et inextrīcābilis error;
examples.english: here the cruel love for the bull ... here that labour of the house, the maze that cannot be untangled

latin: cōnātus erat cāsūs effingere in aurō,
examples.english: twice he had tried to shape the fall in gold, twice the father's hands fell

devices.name: hyperbole
devices.definition: Deliberate exaggeration for effect.

examples.english: she filled up his wounds with tears, and mixed her weeping with his blood
